chief_complaint: jaw pain and swelling directly triggered eating lemon/sour
hpi_details: A 47-year-old male presents to the clinic with jaw pain and swelling directly triggered eating lemon/sour. The patient states the symptoms started recently and have been gradually worsening, accompanied by generalized fatigue.
ideas: He thinks he has an infected tooth root or a swollen gland that flares up whenever acidic food stimulates it.
concerns: He is worried that the tender lump beneath his jaw is a tumor or cancer that will require invasive surgery.
expectations: He hopes to get an ultrasound or scan of his jaw today and anti-inflammatory medicine to bring down the swelling.

core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Submandibular Sialolithiasis is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.
Standard management begins with hydration, sialogogues, salivary massage, and analgesia; persistent, large, or proximally located stones require ENT-directed removal or sialendoscopy.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.

common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Submandibular Sialolithiasis.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Sialadenitis without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Fever with worsening swelling.

reference_soap.subjective: Patient presenting with chief complaint of jaw pain and swelling directly triggered eating lemon/sour. HPI: sialolithiasis.
reference_soap.objective: Focused physical exam and vital signs check. Tailored diagnostics for Submandibular Sialolithiasis.
reference_soap.assessment: Presentation consistent with Submandibular Sialolithiasis: meal-triggered (especially sour/acidic foods) jaw pain and swelling suggesting an obstructing salivary duct stone.
reference_soap.plan: Start hydration, sialogogues, gentle salivary-gland massage, and analgesia. Refer to ENT for ultrasound and sialendoscopy or removal if symptoms persist, the stone is not readily distal/palpable, or infection develops.

must_ask.say: Does swelling start when eating sour food?
How long does swelling last after eating?
Is it under your jaw on one side?
How many times has this happened?

history.answer: Whenever I eat, especially sour foods, the area under my right jaw swells up and aches terribly.
It started about two weeks ago, coming on gradually whenever I sit down to eat.
The pain and swelling are located right under the lower border of my right jaw, occasionally radiating up toward my right ear.
It feels like a tight, throbbing ache with intense pressure under my jaw, reaching around a six out of ten at its peak.
The swelling pops up rapidly while eating, stays swollen for about an hour or two, and then gradually goes down.
It has been getting gradually worse and happening more frequently over the past two weeks.
Sour or acidic foods like lemons, pickles, or salad dressings trigger the swelling almost immediately.
Eating anything tart makes it much worse, while gently massaging the area and drinking water slowly relieves the pressure.
I noticed a milder flare-up a couple of months ago after eating sour candy, but it resolved on its own back then.
No, I have not had any fever, chills, or cold sweats at all.
My mouth feels a little dry at times, and I sometimes notice a slightly salty taste under my tongue, but no bad-tasting pus.
There is a noticeable lump under my right jaw during meals, but my tongue, floor of the mouth, or throat have not swollen up.
No, I can swallow, chew, talk, and breathe without any difficulty.
I have felt a bit more worn out and fatigued recently, but I have not had unexplained weight loss or night sweats.
No, my face feels completely normal, with no drooping, numbness, or muscle weakness.
I have not had any scans, blood tests, or doctor visits for this issue yet.
I took over-the-counter ibuprofen a couple of times, which helped dull the ache a little bit.
It makes eating stressful, so I have been avoiding sour dishes, citrus fruits, and dining out.
I figured an infected tooth root or an inflamed gland was acting up whenever acidic food touched it.
I'm really worried this painful lump under my jaw might be a growing tumor that will need surgery.
I'd like to get an ultrasound or scan of my jaw today to see what is going on and get something to ease the swelling.
I have no chronic medical illnesses like high blood pressure, diabetes, or gout.
I have never had any surgeries and have never been hospitalized.
I do not take any regular prescription medications, vitamins, or herbal supplements.
I do not have any known allergies to medications, foods, or environmental triggers.
I have never smoked cigarettes or used any tobacco products.
I only drink alcohol socially, usually one or two beers on the weekend with friends.
I work as an office manager and live with my wife and our teenage son.
There is no family history of salivary gland disorders, head and neck cancers, or autoimmune diseases.

exam.finding: Blood pressure 120/78 mmHg, heart rate 72 beats/min, respiratory rate 14 breaths/min, temperature 36.6°C, SpO2 99% on ambient air.
Alert, comfortable, well-appearing adult male in no acute distress, with slight visible fullness under the right side of the jaw.
Mild, smooth, tender enlargement of the right submandibular gland on external palpation; no warm overlying erythema or anterior cervical lymphadenopathy.
Bimanual palpation reveals a small, firm, tender palpable mass along the right Wharton duct in the floor of the mouth; duct orifice expresses clear saliva without pus.
Facial movements are symmetric without weakness, sensation across all trigeminal divisions is intact, and tongue protrudes midline.
Both external auditory canals and tympanic membranes are clear without signs of infection or middle ear effusion.
No tenderness upon palpation or percussion over the frontal or maxillary sinuses bilaterally.
Regular rate and rhythm with normal S1 and S2; no murmurs, gallops, or friction rubs heard.
Clear to auscultation bilaterally with normal vesicular breath sounds and no wheezes, crackles, or rhonchi.
